series.title: Reading We Three
series.deck: Four essays on care, unproductive joys, the proportions of memory and a home made by people.

articles.title: A Dream Ten Thousand Li Long
articles.deck: A dream follows the daily route of care and loss.
body: ## A road that was also a timetable

The second part of We Three is called “The Three of Us Are Separated.” Zhongshu is taken away in a vehicle for an unexplained meeting. Yang Jiang and their daughter search until she reaches an old post road governed by peculiar rules: she follows visible paths, does not ask about what she does not know, and returns to an inn by sunset; each day she walks to a boat where Qian Zhongshu lies; she must leave before dark. The next day the boat has moved farther on, so the walk lengthens. Their daughter falls ill inside another dream, and eventually the boat departs beyond reach. This can sound like an allegorical interruption in an otherwise lucid memoir. Read beside the family’s chronology, however, it looks less invented than reported. The road reproduces the shape of Yang’s days.
## Why the dream is the realist section

Qian Zhongshu entered hospital in 1994. Qian Yuan, their only daughter, fell ill at the end of 1995 and entered another hospital early in 1996. Yang Jiang, already in her eighties, travelled between the two, caring for each while concealing the seriousness of the other’s illness. Qian Yuan died in 1997; Qian Zhongshu followed in 1998. The post road translates that routine without reducing it to diagnosis. Its rule against asking resembles the helplessness of medical waiting: one seeks an answer that no answer can make usable. The nightly return resembles visiting hours. The boat moving farther away gives physical distance to decline. The changing inns along the journey capture the absence of any place where the carer may finally settle. These are not decorative symbols placed over experience. They are the experience’s working timetable.
## What a medical record would miss

Yang Jiang was entirely capable of writing the hospital years directly. The last part of the book recounts six decades with precision, naming moves, jobs, shortages and political campaigns. She turns to dream only here because a medical chronology would answer the wrong question. It would tell us how two people died: dates of admission, stages of decline, final symptoms. She wants to record how the survivor lived those years. For her, time did not proceed as a file of events. It became a route that allowed one direction only, demanded another day’s journey and offered no information that could reverse the movement. Calling the section a dream “ten thousand li long” measures both duration and exhaustion. A dream ordinarily ends in waking. Yang wakes to discover that the household to which she might return no longer exists.
## The inn and the rooms they borrowed

Near the end of the dream, Yang calls the family’s home an inn on a journey. The phrase can be generalized into a reflection on transience, but the memoir gives it material force. The family lived in rented Oxford rooms, cramped Shanghai quarters, institutional housing in Beijing, a borrowed office and finally the Sanlihe apartment assigned through work. They moved repeatedly during their shared life. The continuity of home lay not in any one building but in the people living together. A room became home when the three occupied it through breakfast, books, teasing and conversation; after Qian Yuan and Qian Zhongshu were gone, the same walls reverted to being rooms. “Inn” draws force from those repeated moves as well as from the dream. Buildings sheltered them at different stages. The durable form was a relation, and no deed could preserve that form after two of its members disappeared.
## A memoir that gives away its ending first

The book begins with two pages titled “The Two of Us Have Both Grown Old.” Yang dreams that she and Zhongshu are walking together; he vanishes into dusk, she searches and calls, and then wakes. He tells her that old people often have such dreams. This recoverable loss prepares the unrecoverable one in the second part. Only after separation has been completed does the long third part return to the family’s earlier life. The order reverses conventional memoir. Instead of letting affection accumulate until death supplies a climax, Yang announces at the outset: they are gone; I am alone. Every amusing mishap and ordinary meal is then read under knowledge of its ending. The structure is severe, but it is also faithful to the writer’s position. At ninety-two she does not remember forward in innocence. She looks backward from a room in which every remembered day already contains its disappearance.
## A restraint without clenched teeth

Readers often describe the book’s tone as Chinese restraint. That word can imply emotion forced down until it hardens syntax and leaks through pressure. Yang’s sentences do not feel clenched. When Qian Yuan dies, she notes that Zhongshu is still alive and she cannot yet cry; when he dies, she records his last words and continues. But the domestic memories themselves are loose, amused and sometimes delighted. She does not merely suppress grief while performing composure. She shifts attention toward what the grief proves mattered. Zhongshu spills ink, breaks a lamp and damages a hinge; from her hospital bed she answers each report with “Never mind, I can wash it” or “I can mend it.” He believes her completely. Six decades later she still enjoys the scene. The lightness does not deny the loss. It preserves the texture that loss threatens to flatten.
## Counting what cannot be recovered

Yang’s method is to count, one by one, acts that would be zero on any public ledger. A famous scholar makes mistakes in a rented room. A wife reassures him. A child joins private games. None of this explains a book, advances a career or alters history. Yet these are the units in which a vanished home can be remembered. The dream establishes that time carried the three beyond one another’s reach; the rest of the memoir refuses to let that fact monopolize their meaning. Death receives its road, boat and empty inn. Life receives the greater number of pages. That allocation is the first major judgment of We Three: what remains worthy of record is not only how two lives ended, but the countless useless gestures through which three people once inhabited the same world. The next essay follows those gestures and asks what kind of value can survive having no use.

articles.title: Things That Were of No Use
articles.deck: Breakfast, private jokes and three independent lives within one home.
body: ## Breakfast across the years

In their early Oxford days, soon after their marriage, Qian Zhongshu woke before Yang Jiang and attempted breakfast: toast, warm milk, an egg and tea, carried to her bed on a large tray. Yang remembered it as the most fragrant breakfast she had eaten. The experiment became an arrangement. Zhongshu regularly made breakfast through Oxford, the return to China, Shanghai, Beijing and the decades that followed. Yang specifies exceptions: periods in an extended-family household, periods when a maid prepared their meals, and his illnesses. In the social world they inhabited, domestic work by a celebrated male scholar could appear undignified; acquaintances noticed. The couple did not reorganize their morning to satisfy that judgment. The act did not make Zhongshu a better comparatist or produce another volume of scholarship. It made a shared day begin in a particular way. Repeated across decades, a small impropriety became part of the household’s constitution.
## Their expeditions into nowhere

The couple called their walks “expeditions.” In Oxford, Shanghai and Beijing they chose unfamiliar streets, inspected houses and invented biographies for strangers. A hurried passer-by acquired a destination; a couple at a restaurant acquired a quarrel and a history. They jokingly called this practice gewu zhizhi, the classical Confucian project of investigating things and extending knowledge. The disproportion is the joke: one of the most solemn phrases in the intellectual tradition is attached to strolling and making things up. No knowledge is actually certified. The stories are not saved for publication. Their value depends on remaining between the participants, a playful enlargement of the world that produces neither evidence nor credit. By giving the activity a grand name, they do not make it useful. They enjoy the mismatch and create a language whose meaning belongs only to the family.
## Nicknames, painted faces and useless notes

The private language kept multiplying. Husband and wife gave one another nicknames; together they named their daughter. When Qian Yuan was small, her father drew a comic face on her stomach after she fell asleep. His mother scolded him, and he did not dare repeat it. As an adult she remained a companion in teasing. Family letters and remembered jokes preserve reports of foolish behaviour and affectionate mockery, small traces of their daily life. The memoir also remembers meal after meal: improvised cooking in Oxford, shortages in Shanghai, shopping and cooking in Beijing, Qian Yuan coming home to eat. These details occupy more room than public milestones. They do not educate the child in any measurable skill, improve the family’s position or become art outside the household. They are acts whose audience and beneficiary are the same three people.
## Zero on the public ledger

The absence of use becomes striking once we recall who spent the time. Qian Zhongshu wrote Fortress Besieged, Limited Views and scholarship almost no one else could have produced. Yang Jiang became a writer and translator, learning Spanish in her forties before completing her major translation of Don Quixote. Qian Yuan was a respected professor and builder of an English programme. This was a household capable of treating every hour as scarce professional capital. Instead, its members spent large quantities of attention on imagined strangers, private jokes and notes no outsider needed to read. They did so not because work was easy or time abundant. The great books and translations were produced under punishing conditions. Uselessness occupied the intervals deliberately left unconverted. Those intervals were not failed productivity. They were the portion of life that did not have to justify itself through an output.
## Three readers in one room

One of the memoir’s gentlest scenes shows all three reading separately in the same room for hours. It is often admired as an image of cultivated family harmony. Its precise content is stronger: each person has work that matters independently, and the other two do not demand entry into it. Zhongshu’s scholarship, Yang’s translation and Qian Yuan’s teaching are not branches of a single family project. The parents do not require their daughter to reproduce her father’s fame, choose an approved discipline or submit her marriage to their design. Yang writes with pride about Qian Yuan’s teaching, her students and the programme she strengthened, without treating the absence of a monumental book as failure. No one owes the household a performance that will vindicate the name. Their shared silence is therefore not withdrawal. It is a form of company spacious enough for three separate directions.
## The years that demanded a use for everything

The family returned to China during wartime and then lived through campaigns that increasingly required positions, classifications and serviceable explanations. Scholarship needed an approved purpose; associations and reading required accounts; a person’s value had to fit an available category. The memoir narrates 1958, 1966 and the cadre-school years in a notably quiet register. Against that world, it is tempting to transform breakfast and nicknames into heroic resistance. Yang does not. The three did not invent nonsense in order to oppose a regime. They had behaved this way before the campaigns and continued after them. That continuity matters. If the walks had been instruments of resistance, they would have acquired a public use after all. Their distinctive freedom lies in never becoming means. The family kept a region of experience that no questionnaire could describe because it had no strategic point.
## A household without an account to settle

The deepest hospitality of We Three may be its absence of a family ledger. Zhongshu does not have to earn exemption from breakfast by writing great books. Yang’s competence does not license her to direct Qian Yuan’s life. The daughter does not owe achievements proportionate to her parents’ reputation. Each contributes care, work and play, but none is reduced to the balance of contributions. This is why the useless details carry so much weight. A nickname or nonsense note addresses someone without asking what the exchange will yield. It recognizes a person before a function. In decades that repeatedly sought to make the whole individual legible and deployable, the family’s ordinary life remained partly unassignable. The next essay turns to Yang Jiang’s quiet tone about those decades. Its restraint is neither proof that the pain was slight nor evidence that she failed to see it; it is a decision about how much of her own memory public history may occupy.

articles.title: That Quiet Restraint
articles.deck: Quiet narration gives history a place without surrendering the whole of memory.
body: ## A wig, a vegetable plot, a borrowed office

In her separate memoir Bingwu Dingwei Nian Jishi, Yang Jiang records their humiliation in 1966. A cross was shaved into Qian Zhongshu’s hair, and she later shaved the rest clean; she herself was subjected to a half-shaved head. Her practical response was to make a wig from her daughter’s saved braid, using her husband’s hair cap as its base and a small pot as a form. We Three recalls Zhongshu going to a cadre school in Henan and Yang following the next year. In the separate Six Chapters from My Life Downunder, she writes about the vegetable garden and their brief encounters there, keeping attention on daily work and ways of meeting. After returning to Beijing they moved several more times, temporarily staying in an office in 1974; the books moved with them. The facts are not softened. Public humiliation, forced labour, separation and professional interruption are all present. What surprises is the scale of the prose. The wig can sound ingenious, the practical details remain specific, and the catastrophe is not granted a rhetorical climax.
## Two tempting interpretations

That tone invites opposite readings. One praises transcendence: the cultivated intellectual rises above injury, treats honour and disgrace alike and preserves serenity. The other charges evasion: Yang refuses to name perpetrators, passes too quickly over political violence and substitutes domestic charm for judgment. Both readings notice something real and then turn it into a total explanation. The first makes her almost inhuman, as though ordinary fear and damage had been dissolved by wisdom. The second assumes that the only honest relation to historical wrong is explicit indictment in this particular book. A serious reading should not dismiss the ethical force of that demand. Survivors may indeed bear witness, and public memory needs names, causes and verdicts. But before deciding that We Three fails this duty, we must identify what Yang includes, what she withholds and what kind of book she chose to write.
## The facts are present; the verdict is withheld

Yang does not hide suffering. We Three records denunciations, false accusations, banishment, interrupted work and insecure accommodation; the separate memoir supplies the detailed account of the shaved heads and wig. Evasion would require removing the events or disguising their effects. Her selectivity operates elsewhere. She rarely assigns blame, names an offender or expands an incident into a judgment on the age. That silence remains open to criticism; acknowledging her formal choice does not make every consequence beyond debate. Yet it matters that she withholds evaluation rather than evidence. The distinction changes the question. Why would a writer capable of analysis leave the public verdict outside this family memoir? Because once the campaigns become the organising subject, the household becomes an example. Breakfast, notes and walks are demoted to “warmth amid suffering,” valuable mainly for illustrating the cruelty of history. Yang refuses that hierarchy. The private life is not a footnote to the disaster. It is the book’s principal reality.
## Proportion as an argument

The quietness is best understood as proportion. Political campaigns occupy relatively few pages; meals, books, teasing, errands and conversations occupy most of them. This is not a claim that the campaigns were harmless or brief. It is a claim about the total composition of lived time. A denunciation can dominate historical meaning without filling every hour of the day. People still eat, sleep, cultivate a plot, exchange a scrap of paper and look forward to a walk. A passage in Six Chapters from My Life Downunder makes the relation concrete. Zhongshu’s quarters were a little over ten minutes from Yang’s vegetable garden. Serving as a messenger to the post office, he would later often pass the plot. They sat briefly in the sun on the bank of the channel or stood talking; he handed her letters written in fragments. Anxiety and loneliness are not erased, but the narrative continues with what they did within those conditions. The conjunction matters. Misery was real, and so was the rest of life. By controlling the page ratio, she prevents the most coercive force in their environment from becoming the sole author of what those years were.
## Who owns the memory of a life?

If We Three became an indictment, readers might remember the family primarily through what was done to them. Yang asks us to remember how they lived. Both accounts can be true, and other books may properly choose the first. This ninety-two-year-old author claims authority over the distribution within her own recollection. The claim is not that private memory outranks public history or that victims owe nothing beyond themselves. It is narrower: no public interpretation, even a morally correct one, should automatically seize the whole meaning of a life. The decades of campaigns tried to define people by political status and assigned use. A later narrative could repeat that domination in sympathetic form by defining them entirely as victims. Yang’s refusal is not to the truth of victimisation. It is to its demand for narrative monopoly.
## The acts that escaped the forms

During years when scholarship, friendship and thought had to be explained through approved purposes, the family preserved activities for which no form had a box. Inventing a passer-by’s biography, writing nonsense to a daughter, reading different books in one room and preparing breakfast for one’s wife did not serve an institution. They survived partly because they were too small to classify. Yang notes that Zhongshu declined some appointments but also reluctantly accepted a nominal post: after resigning as an adviser to the Institute of Literature in 1982, he became a vice-president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. His resignation a year later was not accepted; he continued to draw a researcher’s salary and kept reading and research at the centre of his life. His recondite textual work scarcely answered the demands of immediate utility. She writes of this in the same register as his household mishaps. The equality of tone is deliberate: neither the scholarship nor the joke needs public necessity to become worthwhile. What totalising systems seek to remove from a person is often precisely this surplus beyond function. We Three restores page after page of that surplus.
## Neither a posture nor an alibi

It would be easy to elevate the family into conscious resisters who protected human freedom through private jokes. Yang’s text does not support that heroic pose. They never announce that strolling or nicknaming will preserve the self. They do these things because they enjoy them, before, during and after political pressure. That purposeless continuity is the point. Turn the acts into resistance and they acquire another instrumental assignment; dismiss the tone as evasion and the public catastrophe once again receives authority to define everything else. Yang’s restraint remains ethically disputable at its edges, but formally it performs a clear act: she records the harm, declines to let it set the scale, and gives the majority of her pages to relations that existed for themselves. The final essay asks what happens when two members of those relations are gone and only one person remains to remember in the plural.

articles.title: I Alone Remember We Three
articles.deck: A solitary writer remembers a shared life whose completed acts remain real.
body: ## Nearly eighteen years after two deaths

Qian Yuan died in 1997 and Qian Zhongshu a little over a year and nine months later, at the end of 1998. Yang Jiang remained in the Sanlihe apartment for nearly another eighteen years and died at 105. She wrote We Three at ninety-two, several years into that solitude. The intervening life was not empty. She sorted sacks of Zhongshu’s reading notes—Chinese and foreign excerpts, annotations and associations in difficult handwriting—into published volumes. The work continued for more than a decade, with later instalments appearing after she had passed one hundred. She translated, wrote Reaching the Brink of Life in her mid-nineties and used the couple’s royalties to establish a scholarship. Organising marginalia could neither restore its author nor greatly increase his reputation. It was the last large-scale version of the family’s useless acts: caring for the traces of another person’s attention because they were what he had left.
## Why write this small book?

Yang gives a modest explanation: she wanted to set down the days when the three were together. She does not claim to provide a national testimony, a model household or the definitive memorial to two eminent intellectuals. The inventory confirms the scale. An Oxford breakfast, biographies invented on a walk, a painted face on a child’s stomach, foolish scraps of paper, spilled ink, a broken lamp, a damaged hinge and the repeated assurance that it could all be mended. A ninety-two-year-old who had lost husband and daughter chose these details over public honours. Their smallness is not camouflage for a grander subject. It is the subject. By writing them one after another, Yang gives durable form to events whose original value lay precisely in not needing an audience beyond the three people present.
## Home was a relation

At the end Yang says their home was only an inn on the road and that she is still searching for the way home. Read abstractly, the lines may sound like a lament about the vanity of earthly attachment. The family’s housing history makes them more concrete. During their shared life they moved repeatedly, from Oxford to Shanghai and Beijing, from temporary rooms to Sanlihe. The addresses changed; continuity was made by the people. The home existed when the relations did. It accumulated through mornings, reading, cooking, teasing, errands and returns. Take away two people and the apartment remains, but the form called home does not. Yang’s search is therefore not for another property or even for a metaphysical answer the memoir could supply. It names the impossibility of locating in space what had always been made through the presence of three particular lives.
## The grammar of “we three”

The third part is titled “I Alone Remember We Three”: in its nine Chinese characters, “I alone” names the present, “we three” the shared decades, and “remember with longing” joins them. The book’s title is not My Husband and Daughter, Remembering Qian Zhongshu or Sixty Years of a Family. “We three” is household speech, an informal name the members used for themselves. Yang places that phrase on the cover after she has become the only living speaker. The grammatical subject of the book is therefore not the survivor alone. Conventional mourning often takes the form “I suffer,” “I lost” or “this was the greatness of the dead.” Yang gives loss its dream in the opening sections, then allows the plural to govern most of the pages. When she remembers Zhongshu’s incompetence with a lamp or Qian Yuan’s teasing, the tone recovers pleasure because the event itself was pleasurable. Grief does not retroactively change the emotional truth of what happened. The singular writer can still testify to a plural past.
## What happened remains happened

The dead are absent, but the breakfast was made, the walk taken, the face drawn and the note answered. None of those events becomes unreal because its participants cannot repeat it. This simple proposition is the memoir’s answer to loss. Yang does not pretend that writing conquers death. The dream states the opposite with brutal clarity: the boat has gone and the inn is empty. Writing cannot bring anyone back or alter the outcome. It can refuse a second erasure in which the end swallows the life that preceded it. The remembered acts retain their own tense and weight. By setting them down, Yang does not make them useful in retrospect; she protects their completed reality. Their value was exhausted in being shared, and precisely for that reason memory must attend to them without demanding a further result.
## A book useful to no one

Measured against Limited Views, Qian Zhongshu’s scholarship or Yang’s translation of Don Quixote, We Three can look minor. It advances no discipline, reverses no death and offers no programme for family life. Even its consolation resists export: readers cannot reproduce these nicknames or inhabit these rooms. Yet among the family’s surviving works, it is the one concerned only with the three as themselves, not as scholar, translator or professor. That exclusivity matters. Public achievement records what their labour contributed to strangers. This thin book records what they were to one another when no contribution was required. Its apparent uselessness is continuous with its content. A work about non-instrumental affection does not need to justify itself by becoming therapeutic instruction or cultural monument. It may remain the place where a private plural is spoken once more.
## The survivor keeps the plural

Across four essays, the pattern comes together. A long dream captures years during which each day lengthened the road toward separation. The remembered decades are filled with acts that produced nothing: a scholar makes breakfast, three readers share a room, family members invent strangers, trade nonsense and preserve paper scraps. History presses for complete accounts of a person’s use; the household keeps what cannot be accounted for. Yang’s quiet tone records injury without surrendering the scale of memory to it. Finally, the survivor asks where home is and cannot locate it because home was never the building. It was the relation named by the book. “I alone remember we three” holds singular and plural in one sentence without resolving their contradiction. One person remains. Three people performed those days. The task of the one is not to replace the three, but to keep their completed life from being rewritten solely as absence.
